steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on end-to-end chess recognition from a single image, which also introduces a new real-image chess recognition dataset.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

  - deep neural network extracts visual features; recognizes board, predicts piece type and position from single image
- ChessReD dataset

  - Chess Recognition Dataset (ChessReD), openly shared
  - 10,800 images + annotations
  - human preference for certain viewpoint possible, but diverse: viewing angles, lighting, camera specs, piece configurations
  - enables further research and realistic benchmark
- Results / contributions

  - ChessReD: first real-image dataset, high viewing angle variability, diverse formations vs synthetic alternatives
  - end-to-end recognition beats sequential pipelines of independent components

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Parsing a chess position from a (smartphone) image makes match analysis easier and helps with coaching children, since it gives chess positions without having to write each move down (Figure 1). To recognize a chess position you need to accurately identify the type and position of each chess piece on a chessboard configuration. The predominant approach is to split this into independent sequential sub-tasks: chessboard detection, square localization, and then piece classification within each square. Our starting point is the observation that these independent sub-tasks suffer from error accumulation through each intermediate independent step. In this paper we get rid of the sequential independent sub-tasks and propose an end-to-end approach for chess recognition, which directly predicts the positions of the pieces, with respect to the chessboard, from the entire image.

One key advantage of our approach is that it doesn't need any human input other than the input image itself. Traditional methods rely on user input, for example manually selecting the corners of the chessboard or defining the player’s perspective. Using a deep neural network, the model can extract and use relevant visual features to recognize the chessboard efficiently, and predict the pieces’ type and positions directly from a single image.

- need a large, good quality dataset; no real-world chess recognition dataset exists
- ChessReD (Chess Recognition Dataset), openly shared; 10,800 images + annotations
- diverse viewing angles, lighting conditions, camera specifications, piece configurations (even though humans may prefer a certain viewpoint)
- results: board recognition accuracy 15.26% (\approx 7x better than state of the art)
- contributions: first real-image dataset (vs synthetic); end-to-end beats sequential pipelines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Parsing a chess position from a (smartphone) image makes match analysis easier and helps with coaching children, since it gives chess positions without having to write each move down (Figure 1). To recognize a chess position you need to accurately identify the type and position of each chess piece on a chessboard configuration. The predominant approach is to split this into independent sequential sub-tasks: chessboard detection, square localization, and then piece classification within each square. Our starting point is the observation that these independent sub-tasks suffer from error accumulation through each intermediate independent step. In this paper we get rid of the sequential independent sub-tasks and propose an end-to-end approach for chess recognition, which directly predicts the positions of the pieces, with respect to the chessboard, from the entire image.

One key advantage of our approach is that it doesn't need any human input other than the input image itself. Traditional methods rely on user input, for example manually selecting the corners of the chessboard or defining the player’s perspective. Using a deep neural network, the model can extract and use relevant visual features to recognize the chessboard efficiently, and predict the pieces’ type and positions directly from a single image.

To evaluate and train our learning-based approach we need a large dataset of good quality. Right now there is no real-world chess recognition dataset, so we introduce our own new real-world Chess Recognition Dataset (ChessReD), and we openly share it with the community. ChessReD has 10,800 images and their annotations, which lets us train and evaluate approaches effectively. There might be a human preference for a certain viewpoint, but we still capture a diverse collection of chessboard images, covering different viewing angles, lighting conditions, camera specifications, and piece configurations. With this dataset there can be further research in chess recognition algorithms and also a realistic benchmark.

On our ChessReD benchmark our approach to chess recognition outperforms related approaches, and gets a board recognition accuracy of 15.26% (\approx 7x better than the current state-of-the-art). Our contributions are:

- • We introduce ChessReD, the first dataset of real images for chess recognition, which has high viewing angle variability and diversity in chess formations compared to synthetic alternatives.

- • We show end-to-end chess recognition that performs better than alternatives which rely on a sequential pipeline of independent components.

The predominant approach [1,2,3,4] is to split this into independent sequential sub-tasks: chessboard detection, square localization, and then piece classification within each square. Our starting point is the observation that these independent sub-tasks suffer from error accumulation through each intermediate independent step. In this paper we get rid of the sequential independent sub-tasks and propose an end-to-end approach for chess recognition, which directly predicts the positions of the pieces, with respect to the chessboard, from the entire image.

One key advantage of our approach is that it doesn't need any human input other than the input image itself. Traditional methods [5,6,7,4] rely on user input, for example manually selecting the corners of the chessboard or defining the player’s perspective. Using a deep neural network, the model can extract and use relevant visual features to recognize the chessboard efficiently, and predict the pieces’ type and positions directly from a single image.

To evaluate and train our learning-based approach we need a large dataset of good quality. Right now there is no real-world chess recognition dataset, so we introduce our own new real-world Chess Recognition Dataset (ChessReD), and we openly share it with the community. ChessReD has 10,800 images and their annotations, which lets us train and evaluate approaches effectively. There might be a human preference for a certain viewpoint [8], but we still capture a diverse collection of chessboard images, covering different viewing angles, lighting conditions, camera specifications, and piece configurations. With this dataset there can be further research in chess recognition algorithms and also a realistic benchmark.

On our ChessReD benchmark our approach to chess recognition outperforms related approaches, and gets a board recognition accuracy of 15.26% (\approx 7x better than the current state-of-the-art). Our contributions are:

- • We introduce ChessReD, the first dataset of real images for chess recognition, which has high viewing angle variability and diversity in chess formations compared to synthetic alternatives.

- • We show end-to-end chess recognition that performs better than alternatives which rely on a sequential pipeline of independent components.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Parsing a chess position from a (smartphone) image eases match analysis and facilitates coaching of children, offering chess positions without writing each move down (Figure 1). Chess position recognition requires accurate identification of each chess piece’s type and position on a chessboard configuration. The predominant approach [1,2,3,4] is to split it into independent sequential sub-tasks: chessboard detection, square localization, and piece classification within each square. We start from the observation that such independent sub-tasks suffer from error accumulation throughout each intermediate independent step. In this paper, we do away with the sequential independent sub-tasks and propose an end-to-end approach for chess recognition, directly predicting the positions of the pieces, with respect to the chessboard, from the entire image.

One key advantage of our approach is that it does not require any human input beyond the input image itself, unlike traditional methods [5,6,7,4] that rely on user input, such as manually selecting the corners of the chessboard or defining the player’s perspective. By using a deep neural network, the model is able to extract and use relevant visual features to efficiently recognize the chessboard and predict the pieces’ type and positions directly from a single image.

To evaluate and facilitate our learning-based approach we need a large, good quality dataset. Currently, there is no real-world chess recognition dataset, and thus we introduce our own real-world Chess Recognition Dataset (ChessReD), which we openly share with the community. ChessReD consists of 10,800 images and their corresponding annotations, allowing us to effectively train and evaluate approaches. Although there might be a human preference for a certain viewpoint [8], we capture a diverse collection of chessboard images, covering various viewing angles, lighting conditions, camera specifications, and piece configurations. This dataset enables further research in chess recognition algorithms as well as a realistic benchmark.

On our ChessReD benchmark, our approach to chess recognition outperforms related approaches, achieving a board recognition accuracy of 15.26% (\approx 7x better than the current state-of-the-art). Our contributions can be summarized as follows.

- • We introduce ChessReD: the first dataset of real images for chess recognition, with high viewing angle variability and diversity in chess formations compared to synthetic alternatives.

- • We demonstrate end-to-end chess recognition with better performance than alternatives that rely on a sequential pipeline of independent components.

References:
[1] Xie et al., 2018a Xie, Y., Tang, G., and Hoff, W. (2018a). Chess piece recognition using oriented chamfer matching with a comparison to cnn. In 2018 IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) , pages 2001–2009. IEEE.
[2] Mehta, 2020 Mehta, A. (2020). Augmented reality chess analyzer (archessanalyzer): In-device inference of physical chess game positions through board segmentation and piece recognition using convolutional neural network. arXiv preprint arXiv:2009.01649 .
[3] Czyzewski et al., 2020 Czyzewski, M. A., Laskowski, A., and Wasik, S. (2020). Chessboard and chess piece recognition with the support of neural networks. Foundations of Computing and Decision Sciences , 45(4):257–280.
[4] Wölflein and Arandjelović, 2021 Wölflein, G. and Arandjelović, O. (2021). Determining chess game state from an image. Journal of Imaging , 7(6):94.
[5] Sokic and Ahic-Djokic, 2008 Sokic, E. and Ahic-Djokic, M. (2008). Simple computer vision system for chess playing robot manipulator as a project-based learning example. In 2008 IEEE International Symposium on Signal Processing and Information Technology , pages 75–79. IEEE.
[6] Ding, 2016 Ding, J. (2016). Chessvision: Chess board and piece recognition. In Tech. rep . Stanford University.
[7] Neto and Campello, 2019 Neto, A. d. S. D. and Campello, R. M. (2019). Chess position identification using pieces classification based on synthetic images generation and deep neural network fine-tuning. In 2019 21st Symposium on Virtual and Augmented Reality (SVR) , pages 152–160. IEEE.
